title: The complete gold setup in *4 steps*
yt_title: The Complete Gold Setup in 4 Steps – Sweep, CHoCH, FVG & Entry Explained

segs.say: Most traders don't lose money in gold because gold is unpredictable – they lose because they enter at the wrong time.
In this video I'll show you a setup in four steps: market structure, liquidity, order blocks and fair value gaps. And at the end we'll put everything together in one example.
Important up front: this is educational content, not investment advice. Trading involves risk of loss – practise new strategies on a demo account first.

chapters.title: Market *structure*
chapters.hook: When is a trend really a trend?

segs.say: Everything starts with market structure. Before you think about an entry, you need to know which way the market is moving.
The market rises and forms a higher high – marked on the chart as H H.
Then comes a pullback. The new low stays above the previous one. That's a higher low, H L.
Now you mark the last high. This is exactly the line that has to break for the trend to be confirmed.
A candle closes above the high: that's a break of structure, or BOS. Pay attention: a wick alone is not enough – the candle close is what counts.
The pattern repeats: a new higher low, a new break of structure. As long as that continues, you only look for buys.

chapters.title: Change of *Character*
chapters.hook: How to spot a trend reversal early

segs.say: But no trend lasts forever. The change of character shows you when the direction is turning.
Here we see a downtrend: lower highs and lower lows.
The last lower high is the key line.
The market makes one more lower low – but the sell-off is getting weaker.
Then a candle closes above the last lower high. That's the change of character – the first hint of a reversal.
The reversal is confirmed by a higher low and a break of structure to the upside. Now the new trend is here.
So remember:
The break of structure confirms the trend.
The change of character warns of a change.

chapters.title: Liquidity & *sweep*
chapters.hook: Why your stop loss always gets hit

segs.say: Step two: liquidity. Big market players need counterparties for their orders – and they find them where lots of stop losses sit.
Here's a clear low. Right below it sit the buyers' stop losses.
Then a second, almost equal low. Equal lows attract liquidity like a magnet.
The wick pokes below. The stops are triggered – and big players buy exactly those sells.
The candle quickly closes back above the low. That was a sweep, not a real breakout.
Then the impulse to the upside follows. Anyone who sold the supposed breakout now becomes fuel for the move.

chapters.title: The *order block*
chapters.hook: This is where big players bought

segs.say: Step three: the order block. It shows you where large orders were placed – and where price often reacts again.
First a move down. Nothing special yet.
Suddenly a strong impulse up. Large orders were in play here.
The last red candle before the impulse is the order block. The zone runs from the low to the high of that candle.
Later, price comes back and tests the zone.
The reaction comes out of the order block. The entry is taken with the stop below the zone.

chapters.title: The *fair value gap*
chapters.hook: This gap acts like a magnet on gold

segs.say: Step four: the fair value gap. It forms when the market moves so fast that it skips prices.
First a quiet market.
Then a huge candle – the market skips several prices.
Between the high of the first candle and the low of the third candle a gap remains. That's the fair value gap.
Gold often comes back to fill this gap.
And from the fair value gap, price then continues in the direction of the trend.

chapters.title: The *complete setup*
chapters.hook: All 4 steps on one gold chart

segs.say: Now let's put it all together – in a buy setup.
On the hourly chart there's an uptrend. On the five-minute chart we see a correction to the downside.
First building block: the sweep. The wick takes the stops below the low.
Second building block: the change of character on the five-minute chart – a close above the last lower high.
The impulse leaves a fair value gap in the discount area. That's your entry zone.
The entry comes on the return into the fair value gap. The stop sits below the sweep wick.
The target is the next high. Important: you calculate the risk-reward ratio before you enter.
A setup is only as good as your risk management.
Risk at most one to two percent of your account per trade.
Set your stop loss before you enter – and don't move it against yourself.
segs.bullet: Set the stop loss before entering

segs.say: Only take trades with a risk-reward ratio of at least one to two.
And no setup works every time. Losses are part of it – what matters is that your winners are bigger than your losers.
